video_title: The Stock Market Is Too Big to Fail | Animal Spirits 492
gist: Recorded the day after a historic rebound, Batnick and Carlson dissect the late-2026 AI crash (S&P -12%, Nasdaq -19.8%, Nvidia -47% after Jensen Huang's resignation) and Nvidia's +31% snapback once Trump helped restore him, arguing 'the stock market is too big to fail' and always forces policy action. They frame the AI trade as 'died, not dead', note cheap valuations (S&P 16x, Nvidia ~8x forward), bonds as the only working hedge, the Anthropic IPO, a restrictive Fed/housing backdrop, and Disney's turnaround.

insights.claim: The late-2026 AI selloff is better described as the AI trade having 'died' (able to come back) than as an AI bubble popping and being dead and buried.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Treat the AI drawdown as a phase change, not terminal; watch for a new leadership phase rather than assuming permanent impairment.
insights.quote: If something died, it can come back.

insights.claim: The AI selloff unfolded in two stages: the midterm election and a data-center slowdown first slowed the trade, then Jensen Huang's resignation from Nvidia derailed it entirely.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Key-man and political events, not fundamentals alone, were the proximate catalysts; monitor leadership/political headlines for AI names.

insights.claim: Hedge fund pod shops used the Jensen news as an excuse to de-risk after big gains and fading momentum, while retail traders kept buying until they too capitulated late in the week.
insights.speaker: co-host (Michael Batnick or Ben Carlson)
insights.so_what: Positioning washouts can be excuse-driven; flows rather than news may explain the size of the move.
insights.quote: All the all the hedge fund pod shops took their risk down.

insights.claim: At Friday's lows the S&P 500 was down 11.6% (about 12% from highs) and the Nasdaq 19.8%, just shy of a bear market; the S&P went from +15% YTD in October to +2%, and the Nasdaq from +24% YTD to negative in six weeks.
insights.speaker: co-host (Michael Batnick or Ben Carlson)
insights.so_what: Recent corrections keep stopping just short of -20% (2018, Liberation Day, now); a pattern of near-bear-markets.

insights.claim: Mag Seven drawdowns at the lows: Nvidia about -47%, Google -33%, Meta and Tesla nearly -30%; some neoclouds fell 60-80%.
insights.speaker: co-host (Michael Batnick or Ben Carlson)
insights.so_what: Neoclouds were the epicenter of the data-center bubble deflation; mega-caps fell far less.

insights.claim: During the AI crash nearly everything else fell too (EM -21% into a bear market, EFA -10%, Russell 2000 -16%, gold, silver, Bitcoin), and core bonds were the only widely held hedge that worked; managed futures did okay but few investors own them.
insights.speaker: co-host (Michael Batnick or Ben Carlson)
insights.so_what: Do not count on gold or crypto as equity hedges in a risk-off liquidation; high-quality bonds remained the reliable diversifier.
insights.quote: The only thing that stopped you was bonds.

insights.claim: The S&P 500 fell 8.6% in one week, one of the worst weeks of the decade; per Bespoke it was only the sixth time since WWII the index fell all five days with at least four 1% drops, and it closed four standard deviations below its 50-day moving average, the most oversold since the 2015 yuan devaluation.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Extreme oversold readings historically precede decent forward returns; a reference point for capitulation.

insights.claim: Ryan Dietrich's data show the faster a 10% correction happens (this one took 33 trading days), the less likely it becomes a full bear market; V-shaped first legs tend not to reach -20%.
insights.speaker: co-host (Michael Batnick or Ben Carlson)
insights.so_what: Speed of decline argues against a full bear market; use as a probabilistic tilt toward buying.

insights.claim: When the VIX hits roughly 40, forward equity returns have been very good, and Michael's rule is to buy when people panic.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: VIX spikes to ~40 are historically buy signals for long-horizon investors.
insights.quote: When the VIX hits like the bucket that it was in it hit 40 briefly. Forward returns are very good.

insights.claim: Michael bought DRAM and SMH (semiconductor ETFs) around Friday lunchtime during the panic and sold at Monday's open after the rebound; Ben also added to beaten-down names.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Hosts acted on their 'forced to buy panics' rule; short-term trades in memory/semis captured the snapback.

insights.claim: A correction now is healthier than a fourth straight 20%+ up year after Nasdaq gains of 55% (2023), 25% (2024) and 20% (2025).
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Resetting excess after serial big years reduces future fragility; don't fear the reset.

insights.claim: The AI drawdown is a good fire drill to reassess risk tolerance: if you panicked, de-risk modestly (e.g., 70/30 to 60/40) at 12% off the highs rather than panic to cash; it is not too late since the market isn't down 40%.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Use rebounds as a 'get out of jail free card' to right-size equity exposure and concentrated positions.
insights.quote: That's never a good idea to panic go to cash.

insights.claim: Concentrated winners should consider selling despite taxes; paying taxes means you won, and a trader's account that fell from $27 million to $577,000 shows how fast leveraged gains unwind.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Tax-lock is a common reason for dangerous concentration; trim when a 40% single-stock weight scares you.
insights.quote: if you're paying taxes on an investment, guess what that means? You won.

insights.claim: The 3x leveraged semiconductor ETF SOXL had $35 billion at its June peak, now under $10 billion, and fell 88% from its highs.
insights.speaker: co-host (Michael Batnick or Ben Carlson)
insights.so_what: Leveraged-ETF AUM collapse is a capitulation marker for retail semis speculation.

insights.claim: Neither host expects new S&P all-time highs by year-end (Michael would need 8-to-1 odds to bet on it); if they come, the first half of 2027 is more likely than the second half.
insights.speaker: co-host (Michael Batnick or Ben Carlson)
insights.so_what: Expect choppy consolidation into year-end with a recovery to highs in H1 2027 as the base case.

insights.claim: Michael does not think the bull market is over: there's still too much muscle memory, it's early in the cycle, demand is intact, and the next earnings season will show 'insane' numbers that make investors realize they got too bearish.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Position for an earnings-driven re-rating of beaten-down AI names trading at single-digit multiples.
insights.quote: I don't think the bull market's over.

insights.claim: Every sector saw multiple compression in 2026 despite strong earnings: tech multiple down 43% with 75% earnings growth, communication services down 31% with 23% earnings growth.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Price has de-rated far more than fundamentals; the market is 'doing the worrying for you'.
insights.quote: Technology stocks, the multiple is down 43% this year.

insights.claim: As of the Friday lows, the S&P 500 traded at 16x forward earnings (back near Liberation Day lows) and small and mid caps at 12-13x forward earnings, which the hosts call cheap.
insights.speaker: co-host (Michael Batnick or Ben Carlson)
insights.so_what: Broad market and especially small/mid caps offer value entry points; the open question is whether earnings persist.
insights.quote: The stock market is cheap.

insights.claim: Nvidia's forward P/E fell to about 8x, a valuation no one would have predicted in an 'AI bubble'; Ben argues the revealed key-man and government risk justify no more than ~10x forward earnings.
insights.speaker: co-host (Michael Batnick or Ben Carlson)
insights.so_what: Nvidia may be structurally de-rated for governance/political risk even as revenue soars; size accordingly.
insights.quote: who would have ever thought in an AI bubble that Nvidia would trade at eight times earnings?

insights.claim: Valuations are not a short-term catalyst; over the next week to six months, flows and technicals completely dwarf fundamentals.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Don't expect cheapness alone to stop a selloff; time entries using flows/oversold signals.

insights.claim: The best bear case on AI (from Kadroski via Derek Thompson): AI has saturated coder demand and captured the low-hanging fruit, so revenue extrapolations may be too high and there may be no next wave of mass enterprise/consumer adoption, making ~$1.5 trillion valuations too big.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Watch enterprise adoption beyond coding as the swing factor for AI-lab and infrastructure valuations.
insights.quote: They've saturated the demand for coders

insights.claim: Private markets don't know how to value companies: big tech IPOs since 2012 (CrowdStrike, CoreWeave, Shopify) typically pop in week one then crash about 50% within the first year; Kalshi seeking a $60-65 billion valuation is cited as excessive.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Avoid chasing hot tech IPOs early; better entry points often come within the first year.
insights.quote: I don't think people in the private markets know how to value companies.

themes.theme: Nvidia, Jensen Huang and the government put

insights.claim: Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO, after the board said it would not reinstate him, followed a call from President Trump assuring there was no national-security problem; Nvidia rose 31% in one day to about $4 trillion but remained down 30%+ from highs.
insights.speaker: co-host (Michael Batnick or Ben Carlson)
insights.so_what: Political intervention can reverse corporate governance decisions overnight; event risk cuts both ways.

insights.claim: The stock market always gets what it wants (TARP 2008, COVID, Liberation Day, now Nvidia): severe enough declines force government action, so 'the stock market is too big to fail'.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Assume a policy put under large drawdowns; tail-hedging pays less often than in a world without intervention.
insights.quote: The stock market always gets what it wants.

insights.claim: With roughly 60% to two-thirds of US households owning stocks, the market is more politically important than ever, so authorities will do everything to save it when something bad happens.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Broad equity ownership raises the probability and speed of policy rescues.

insights.claim: Tech and semis were down an average of 26% even after the bounce while the S&P was down only 8%; had tech/semis fallen 40-45%, sentiment would have infected the whole market.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Sector contagion threshold matters; monitor tech/semis drawdown depth as a market-wide risk gauge.

insights.claim: Semiconductors fell from 19% of the S&P 500 in summer to 12%; the market surviving that is a 'miracle', but a drop to 8% might not be withstandable.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Semis' index weight is a key systemic variable for the S&P.

insights.claim: Nvidia's extreme dependence on one person reveals large key-man risk that is bearish for its multiple; Dan Ives estimated Jensen was worth about $1 trillion to Nvidia, which Monday's move roughly confirmed.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Founder-led mega-caps carry a hidden key-man discount; price it in.
insights.quote: isn't it a little bearish that one person has to be so important to this technology?

insights.claim: Open questions after the reversal include whether the SEC probe into Nvidia's accounting disappears and whether roughly 20% of Nvidia's business allegedly going to China through the back door is lost.
insights.speaker: co-host (Michael Batnick or Ben Carlson)
insights.so_what: Residual regulatory and China revenue risks remain unresolved despite the rally.

insights.claim: Nvidia hit its most oversold level since 2008 on 14-day RSI after a late-Friday headline about an SEC accounting probe sent it down another 10-15%.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Extreme RSI readings marked the bottom here; a useful capitulation signal.

insights.claim: Markets ignore risks until narratives catch fire: an Oct. 29 NYT story on Jensen as target of a Chinese spy plot moved Nvidia only 80 bps with VIX at 17, weeks before the same theme crashed the stock.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Early under-reacted headlines can be leading indicators; track dismissed stories for latent tail risk.
insights.quote: This story broke on October 29th and for whatever reason nobody cared.

insights.claim: Government intervention favoring the powerful is bullish short-term but risks a political snapback: hearings and regulation could follow the current anything-goes deregulation phase.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Price a future regulatory backlash risk into AI/mega-cap holdings over a multi-year horizon.
insights.quote: I don't think people realize what the snap back could be from the other side.

insights.claim: Monday's rebound was a 'reverse 1987 crash': Nvidia +31%, Dell 20%+, SK Hynix +20%, Micron +18%, and SanDisk, which had been -70% from its highs at the lows, still up 170% YTD.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Memory and AI-hardware names have extreme two-way volatility; size positions for crash-up and crash-down days.

themes.theme: Anthropic IPO, AI adoption and AI risk

insights.claim: Anthropic's IPO was oversubscribed despite the worst AI sentiment ever, valuing a company founded in January 2021 at about $1.5 trillion; shares opened at $81 (~$1.1 trillion), almost 20% off the highs.
insights.speaker: co-host (Michael Batnick or Ben Carlson)
insights.so_what: Strong primary demand despite sentiment lows signals institutional conviction in frontier labs.
insights.quote: they go from being worth $0 to being worth $1.5 trillion when they IPO.

insights.claim: AI breakthroughs are accelerating (e.g., an Anthropic researcher used Claude to solve a math hypothesis a Cornell professor called 'Mount Olympus') even as AI stock sentiment hit lows, a divergence that only makes sense via second-order effects on employment and the economy.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Technology progress and stock sentiment are diverging; a potential long-term opportunity if second-order fears are overdone.

insights.claim: AI is moving through phases: phase one was LLMs and chatbots, phase two is agents (e.g., Meta's Muse doing tasks like securing airline refunds), and phase three is likely robotics over the next decade.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Shift attention to agent-enabled platforms and later robotics as the next AI investment phases.
insights.quote: Phase one was LLMs and chatbots. Phase two is agents.

insights.claim: Meta's Muse agent is growing quickly (DAUs ~10 million) and the hosts expect it to beat a rival app ('Instinct'), as Meta can run it unprofitably for a long time; Ben notes Meta seems to realize users need useful products, not frontier-scale models.
insights.speaker: co-host (Michael Batnick or Ben Carlson)
insights.so_what: Scale incumbents with cash flows can outlast venture-backed AI apps; favor distribution over model size.
insights.quote: Meta doesn't have to make any money on news for a very long time.

insights.claim: AI may become the greatest narrative-transmission engine ever, creating 'herds of turbo sheep' that move faster and harder in one direction (Orbis white paper), so cycles will keep accelerating.
insights.speaker: co-host (Michael Batnick or Ben Carlson)
insights.so_what: Expect faster boom-bust cycles and sharper crowding; widen risk limits and act faster on dislocations.
insights.quote: AI may simply create herds of turbo sheep

insights.claim: Hedge funds unloaded tech over six weeks in a near four-sigma event, twice the prior record (Marlon Capital data); hedge funds now behave like retail and are the herd, not contrarians.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Don't rely on 'smart money' as stabilizers; their crowded exits amplify moves.
insights.quote: They're not contrarians anymore. They are the herd.

insights.claim: A frontier lab's model going rogue or an AI-linked hack would be a huge stock-market risk, both morally and via regulation destroying earnings power; recent widespread outages appear more like AI-introduced bugs than hacking per a software engineer listener.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: AI-safety incidents are a tail risk for AI equities; monitor outage attribution and regulatory responses.

insights.claim: Viral wealth from the Anthropic IPO (600 employees worth $100M+, more than in all of Los Angeles) is fueling inequality anger that is showing up in elections, raising the question of whether capitalism has gone too far.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Inequality backlash is a political risk vector for AI companies and tax policy.

themes.theme: Macro: Fed, inflation, financial conditions, housing

insights.claim: Goldman Sachs' US financial conditions index (ex-equities) shows restrictive conditions from cost of capital and inflation, a big reason precious metals and crypto did poorly and investors were eager to de-risk.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Tight financial conditions explain non-AI asset weakness; easing would be a cross-asset tailwind.

insights.claim: Fed Governor Waller floated a half-point rate hike to shock inflation, but the equity selloff lowered rate-hike odds; markets had priced ~88% for a December move, which Michael doubts will happen.
insights.speaker: co-host (Michael Batnick or Ben Carlson)
insights.so_what: Watch December FOMC; the stock market may be 'doing the Fed's job', reducing hike probability.
insights.quote: the stock market is doing the Fed's job for it.

insights.claim: Ben argues inflation around 3.5% with 4% unemployment and ~7% nominal GDP is not dire and fears the Fed overshoots trying to reach 2%; Michael counters that inflation is still a problem as the last four to five years ran well above the 100-year average.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Policy overshoot risk is a key macro downside; inflation persistence is the counter-risk.

insights.claim: Stock-market wealth effects and consumer spending now matter more for consumer prices than Fed rate hikes.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Equity drawdowns may cool inflation faster than rate policy; watch market levels for inflation outlook.

insights.claim: The housing market is still dead: homebuilder confidence is back to 2012 levels, 46% of builders cut prices in November (largest share post-pandemic per Neil Dutta), building permits hit a post-pandemic low, and house-flipping ROI has crashed (Texas a 'wasteland').
insights.speaker: co-host (Michael Batnick or Ben Carlson)
insights.so_what: Housing remains a drag on employment and activity; homebuilder margins under pressure from price cuts.
insights.quote: Homebuilder confidence is back to 2012 levels.

insights.claim: Crypto 'died' but isn't dead: Bitcoin fell back under $60,000 with one of the largest monthly declines in Bitcoin ETF holdings, and bleak sentiment is generally a contrarian signal that selling is near an end.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Extreme crypto pessimism may mark late-stage selling; catalysts remain absent.
insights.quote: bleak is good, generally speaking.

insights.claim: Michael bought Disney after years of 'dead money' because EPS is breaking out: Marvel drove 2.6 billion streaming hours in 2026, and ESPN NFL/college viewership hit records (Monday Night Football up 24% season to date).
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Disney's earnings inflection and live-sports strength support a turnaround thesis.
insights.quote: I'm back. I bought Disney.

insights.claim: Sports are the last monoculture: 95 of the top 100 shows are sports (Andy Jassy), and streamers will take an increasing share of NFL rights even as ESPN linear subscribers decline.
insights.speaker: co-host (Michael Batnick or Ben Carlson)
insights.so_what: Live sports rights are the key moat; favor platforms securing them as linear TV melts.

insights.claim: GTA VI generated about $3.7-3.79 billion on day one including pre-orders, out-grossing Avengers Endgame and the last two Avatar films, after reportedly $1.5 billion and 13 years of development.
insights.speaker: co-host (Michael Batnick or Ben Carlson)
insights.so_what: The gaming market's scale dwarfs film; big franchise releases are massive revenue events for publishers.
